Passage: Storm over the Kestrel.
Scene: A suspenseful but child-friendly adventure scene at night aboard a large elongated dirigible AIRSHIP flying over a dark ocean during rain. Twelve-year-old GIRL Nell Varga crouches low on a narrow metal exterior catwalk, wearing a clearly visible safety harness securely CLIPPED to a taut safety line. One hand holds the protective railing; the other reaches toward the loose canvas cargo cover and its iron fastening ring. A few plain wooden medicine crates are sheltered beneath the cover. The airship's massive curved metallic hull, small round portholes and rigging define the scene; the ship has an elongated gas envelope and gondola, not a hot-air balloon basket. Wind ruffles her jacket, storm clouds and silver wave crests below convey suspense. Her face shows focus and courage, not screaming. Keep her body supported on the catwalk with the harness unmistakable, no fall or injury. No text or medical symbols on the crates, no giant bee, no literal monster mouth in the sea.

Passage: The Garden Behind the Wall.
Scene: A tender scene from a garden play, six weeks after spring begins. Eleven-year-old GIRL Rosa and her young male neighbor Theo kneel beside newly planted beds in a yard behind an old stone house. Pink roses climb the high stone wall, the rusty gate stands open, and young plants replace the old dead vines. Grandma Ines sits on a garden bench with her walking cane resting safely beside her; she reaches for a packet of seeds offered by Rosa and holds a small trowel, joining the children's work. Rosa has a little soil on her nose and a hopeful happy expression. Warm light and connection across three generations. Show the exact trio, no other elderly neighbor, no rooftop, no hidden treasure, no gardening machinery or readable writing. A soft hint of theatrical red curtain at the far upper corners may suggest the play, but keep the living garden scene dominant.

Passage: How a Seed Wakes Up.
Scene: A clear natural-history storybook illustration of seed germination in a spring garden. A continuous soil cross-section shows FOUR successive small plants arranged naturally from left to right: a dormant intact brown seed; a swollen seed whose coat is splitting with the first white ROOT pointing DOWN; a root growing deeper while a curled green SHOOT bends UP toward the soil surface; and a seedling above ground with its first pair of green leaves unfolded and branching roots below. Gentle rain droplets soak the soil at one side and warm sunshine reaches the leaves at the other, with a little receding winter frost at the far edge. Plausible botanical anatomy and scale, no human faces, no magical eye, no labels, diagrams with words, arrows or numbers. The shoot and root must emerge in the right directions; do not depict a leaf sprouting from an unsplit closed seed.
